---
title: "Structural identification in BVARs"
subtitle: "Lecture 7"
---

## Overview

By the end of this lecture you can take a well-forecasting vector autoregression and
ask it what an unexpected policy tightening does, and say precisely which part of the
answer came from the data and which part you assumed.

::: {.callout-important}
## The result of this chapter

Reduced-form innovations $u_t$ with covariance $\Sigma$ are linear combinations of
uncorrelated unit-variance structural shocks $\varepsilon_t$ through an impact matrix,

$$
u_t = B_0\varepsilon_t, \qquad \Sigma = B_0B_0^\top,
$$

and the impulse response of the system at horizon $h$ is $\Psi_h B_0$, with $\Psi_h$ the
reduced-form moving-average coefficients. The difficulty is that the second equation has
more unknowns than equations: the likelihood fixes $\Sigma$ and leaves an entire
orthogonal group of impact matrices to choose from, so the map from reduced form to
structural form must be closed by an assumption that no amount of data can supply.
:::

After working through this chapter you can

1. diagnose why the reduced-form likelihood leaves the impact matrix undetermined, and
   count the free dimensions;
2. derive the recursive identification scheme as the unique triangular square root of
   the covariance, and show how a reordering changes it;
3. derive the accept-reject rotation sampler for sign restrictions, including why the
   rotation must be drawn uniformly on the orthogonal group;
4. implement both schemes on posterior draws from a Bayesian vector autoregression in
   Python, and produce impulse responses with credible bands;
5. compare the answers the two schemes give on identical reduced-form estimates, and
   interpret the difference as the price of an assumption;
6. interpret a sign-restricted band as set identification, distinguishing the part that
   shrinks with the sample from the part that does not.

Week 7 of 15, paired with the [Week 7 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/07-bvar-identification.qmd). The chapter assumes the
Minnesota prior and the shrinkage results of Lecture 6, the Gibbs sampler of Lecture 4
and the accept-reject argument of Lecture 3.

## Motivation: the forecast is good and no shock has a name {#sec-motivation}

Lecture 6 left a vector autoregression in industrial production growth, consumer price
inflation and the federal funds rate that forecasts better than least squares at every
horizon and better than a random walk almost everywhere. A central bank now asks the
question it actually has: if we raise the rate by a quarter point for reasons unrelated
to what we already know about output and prices, what happens to output and prices?

The model appears to contain the answer and does not. The difficulty is visible in the
raw data before any estimation. Inflation and the policy rate rise together and fall
together, which is exactly what one would see if tightening caused inflation, and also
exactly what one would see if the central bank raised rates in response to inflation.
The estimated system does not adjudicate, because it was never asked to: each equation
is a forecasting regression, and the residuals of the three equations are correlated
with one another, so a surprise in the rate equation arrives in the same month as
surprises in the other two. The chunk below estimates the reduced form on the panel of
@sec-data and looks at those residuals.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

DATA = next(p for p in (Path("data"), Path("../data")) if p.exists())
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})

fred = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "fred_macro_monthly.parquet")
mac = pd.DataFrame({
    "ip_growth": 100 * np.log(fred["industrial_prod"]).diff(),
    "inflation": 100 * np.log(fred["cpi"]).diff(),
    "fed_funds": fred["fed_funds"],
}).dropna().loc["1960-02":"2019-12"]
var_names, m_var, p_var = list(mac.columns), 3, 12

def build_var_xy(data, p):                 # stacked regression form of a VAR(p)
    T, m = data.shape
    Y = data[p:]
    X = np.ones((T - p, 1 + m * p))
    for ell in range(1, p + 1):
        X[:, 1 + (ell - 1) * m: 1 + ell * m] = data[p - ell: T - ell]
    return X, Y

D_var = mac.to_numpy()
X_var, Y_var = build_var_xy(D_var, p_var)
T_eff, k_var = X_var.shape
B_ols = np.linalg.solve(X_var.T @ X_var, X_var.T @ Y_var)
U_ols = Y_var - X_var @ B_ols
Sigma_ols = U_ols.T @ U_ols / (T_eff - k_var)
corr_u = np.corrcoef(U_ols.T)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.0))
roll = mac[["inflation", "fed_funds"]].rolling(12).mean().dropna()
axes[0].plot(roll.index, 12 * roll["inflation"], color="firebrick",
             label="inflation, annualised 12-month mean")
axes[0].plot(roll.index, roll["fed_funds"], color="steelblue", label="federal funds rate")
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.7)
axes[0].set_ylabel("percent"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_title("They move together, and nothing says why")

axes[1].scatter(U_ols[:, 2], U_ols[:, 0], s=9, alpha=0.5)
axes[1].axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.7); axes[1].axvline(0, color="black", lw=0.7)
axes[1].set_xlabel("funds rate equation residual")
axes[1].set_ylabel("output equation residual")
axes[1].set_title(f"Correlated surprises, r = {corr_u[0, 2]:.3f}")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{len(mac)} months, {mac.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {mac.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(f"T_eff = {T_eff}, k = {k_var} per equation, {k_var * m_var} in the system")
print("residual standard deviations:", np.round(np.sqrt(np.diag(Sigma_ols)), 4))
print("reduced-form residual correlations:")
print(pd.DataFrame(corr_u, index=var_names, columns=var_names).round(3))
```

The left panel is the identification problem as an economist meets it. The annualised
twelve-month mean of inflation and the federal funds rate trace nearly the same path for
sixty years: both climb through the 1970s, both collapse after 1982, both sit near zero
after 2009. A correlation of that size between a policy instrument and a policy target
is consistent with an aggressive central bank that causes inflation and with a
responsive central bank that chases it, and the series alone cannot separate them.

The right panel is the same problem as a statistician meets it. The one-step forecast
errors of the output equation and the funds rate equation correlate at $0.180$; inflation
and the funds rate at $0.053$; output and inflation at $0.016$. These are not
independent surprises that can be labelled one per equation. A month in which the funds
rate came in above its forecast is a month in which output tended to come in above its
forecast too, and no reduced-form quantity says whether the rate moved because output
did, or output moved because the rate did, or a third thing moved both.

It is worth being precise about what is being asked for, because the phrase monetary
policy shock is doing a lot of work. The federal funds rate moves for two kinds of reason.
Most of its variation is systematic: the committee follows a rule, explicit or not, that
responds to the state of the economy, and that response is already inside the estimated
coefficients of the funds rate equation. What is left over is the part of this month's
rate that the rule and the history do not explain, and only that part is a candidate for a
shock. The question the central bank asked is about the second kind of movement, and the
reduced form does contain a residual that is the right size. What it does not contain is
any reason to believe that residual is a policy surprise rather than a mixture of the
three surprises hitting the economy that month.

That is the breakdown. The shrunk system of Lecture 6 is an excellent description of the
joint forecast distribution and contains no object called a monetary policy shock. The
next section shows that this is not a matter of estimating something more carefully: the
missing object is not weakly identified but completely unidentified, and the sample size
is irrelevant to it.

## The problem: the covariance does not determine the impact matrix {#sec-problem}

Structural shocks $\varepsilon_t$ are defined to be mutually uncorrelated with unit
variance, so they can be interpreted one at a time. They are linked to the innovations
by an impact matrix, $u_t = B_0\varepsilon_t$, and taking the covariance of both sides
gives $\Sigma = B_0B_0^\top$. Everything the likelihood knows about $B_0$ is in that
equation, and it is not enough.

### Result R-7.1: the rotation ambiguity

Let $\Sigma$ be an $m \times m$ symmetric positive definite matrix and let $B_0$ satisfy
$\Sigma = B_0B_0^\top$. Then for every orthogonal $Q$, that is every $Q$ with $QQ^\top =
I_m$,

$$
(B_0Q)(B_0Q)^\top = B_0QQ^\top B_0^\top = B_0B_0^\top = \Sigma ,
$$

so $B_0Q$ is also an impact matrix, and conversely every matrix $\tilde B_0$ with
$\tilde B_0\tilde B_0^\top = \Sigma$ is of that form. The set of solutions is therefore
exactly one orbit of the orthogonal group, of dimension

$$
m^2 - \frac{m(m+1)}{2} = \frac{m(m-1)}{2},
$$

which is three for $m = 3$. The likelihood $L(B,\Sigma \mid Y)$ does not involve $B_0$ at
all, so it is constant along the orbit, while the structural impulse responses
$\Psi_h B_0 Q$ are not. No sample size changes this: as $T \to \infty$ the posterior for
$\Sigma$ concentrates on a point and the orbit above that point stays exactly as large as
it was.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

The forward direction is the display above. For the converse, suppose $B_1$ and $B_2$
both satisfy $B_iB_i^\top = \Sigma$. Since $\Sigma$ is positive definite each $B_i$ is
invertible, so set $Q = B_1^{-1}B_2$. Then

$$
QQ^\top = B_1^{-1}B_2B_2^\top B_1^{-\top} = B_1^{-1}\Sigma B_1^{-\top}
= B_1^{-1}B_1B_1^\top B_1^{-\top} = I_m ,
$$

so $Q$ is orthogonal and $B_2 = B_1Q$. The solution set is thus $\{B_1Q : QQ^\top = I_m\}$,
a single orbit.

For the count, $\Sigma$ is symmetric and so has $m(m+1)/2$ distinct entries, giving that
many equations, while $B_0$ has $m^2$ unknowns. The shortfall is $m^2 - m(m+1)/2 =
m(m-1)/2$, which is precisely the dimension of the orthogonal group $O(m)$: an orthogonal
matrix has $m$ columns constrained to unit length and $m(m-1)/2$ pairwise orthogonality
constraints, leaving $m^2 - m - m(m-1)/2 = m(m-1)/2$ free parameters. The two counts agree
because the map $Q \mapsto B_0Q$ is a bijection from $O(m)$ onto the solution set.

Why the likelihood cannot help. Write the model as $Y = XB + U$ with the rows of $U$
independent $\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)$. The likelihood is

$$
L(B,\Sigma \mid Y, X) \propto |\Sigma|^{-T_{\text{eff}}/2}
\exp\left\{-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}\left[\Sigma^{-1}(Y-XB)^\top(Y-XB)\right]\right\},
$$

a function of $(B,\Sigma)$ only. The symbol $B_0$ does not appear, because the data are
the $y_t$ and the $y_t$ depend on the structural shocks only through $u_t = B_0\varepsilon_t$,
whose distribution is $\mathcal{N}(0, B_0B_0^\top)$ and therefore depends on $B_0$ only
through $\Sigma$. In the language of identification, $(B,\Sigma)$ is the identified
parameter and $B_0$ is a function of it only after a further restriction is imposed; the
likelihood is flat in the three remaining directions, so the posterior in those directions
is exactly the prior, whatever prior is placed there. This is the sense in which the
problem is not weak identification. Weak identification means a likelihood with a shallow
but genuine peak, improved by more data. Here there is no peak at all.

One structural consequence is worth recording now, because R-7.3 depends on it. Since
every $B_0Q$ fits equally well, restricting attention to a subset of the orbit is not a
statistical estimate but a choice of subset, and the honest report is both the subset and
what remains inside it. The two schemes of the next section differ in exactly this: one
chooses a single point of the orbit, the other a region of it.
:::

The result is checkable, so the chunk below checks it. It takes the least-squares
reduced-form estimate, draws two hundred rotations at random, and traces the implied
response of output growth to the first structural shock.

```{python}
#| label: fig-orbit
#| fig-cap: "Two hundred impact matrices, all reproducing the same estimated residual covariance exactly, and the responses of output growth they imply for the first structural shock."
def companion(B, m, p):
    C = np.zeros((m * p, m * p))
    for ell in range(p):
        C[:m, ell * m:(ell + 1) * m] = B[1 + ell * m: 1 + (ell + 1) * m, :].T
    if p > 1:
        C[m:, :m * (p - 1)] = np.eye(m * (p - 1))
    return C

def irf(B, impact, H, m, p):
    C = companion(B, m, p)
    out = np.zeros((H + 1, m, m))
    Ch = np.eye(m * p)
    for h in range(H + 1):
        out[h] = Ch[:m, :m] @ impact
        Ch = Ch @ C
    return out

def haar_rotation(m, rng):
    Qm, Rm = np.linalg.qr(rng.standard_normal((m, m)))
    return Qm * np.sign(np.diag(Rm))               # uniform on the orthogonal group

H_orbit = 36
P_chol = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma_ols)
paths, fit_err, imp0 = [], [], []
for _ in range(200):
    Bq = P_chol @ haar_rotation(m_var, rng)
    fit_err.append(np.abs(Bq @ Bq.T - Sigma_ols).max())
    imp0.append(Bq[0, 0])
    paths.append(np.cumsum(irf(B_ols, Bq, H_orbit, m_var, p_var)[:, 0, 0]))
paths = np.array(paths)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for row in paths:
    ax.plot(np.arange(H_orbit + 1), row, color="steelblue", lw=0.6, alpha=0.35)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.9)
ax.set_xlabel("horizon (months)"); ax.set_ylabel("IP level response (%)")
ax.set_title("One reduced form, two hundred structural answers")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"largest |B0 B0' - Sigma| over the 200 rotations: {max(fit_err):.3e}")
print(f"impact response of IP growth, range over rotations: "
      f"[{min(imp0):.4f}, {max(imp0):.4f}]")
print(f"IP level response at h = 12, range over rotations: "
      f"[{paths[:, 12].min():.4f}, {paths[:, 12].max():.4f}]")
print(f"share of rotations with a negative IP level at h = 12: "
      f"{(paths[:, 12] < 0).mean():.3f}")
```

Every one of the two hundred impact matrices reproduces the estimated covariance to
$4.996 \times 10^{-16}$, which is machine precision, so all two hundred fit the data
identically and the likelihood cannot rank them. The responses they imply do not agree at
all. The impact effect on output growth runs from $-0.6608$ to $0.6498$, and the level of
industrial production one year after the shock ranges from $-1.3770$ percent to $1.3586$
percent, with $56.0$ percent of the rotations giving a fall and the rest a rise. The
figure is that set drawn: a fan covering both signs at every horizon, every line of which
is an exactly equally good description of sixty years of monthly data.

This is worth being clear about, because it is easy to mistake for a small-sample
complaint. The bundle of lines above would not thin out with a thousand years of data. It
is the identified object, $\Sigma$, mapping onto an unidentified one. The repair cannot
therefore be statistical, and the next section supplies two versions of the only kind of
repair available.

## Methodology: two ways to cut the orbit down {#sec-methodology}

Identification means adding restrictions that select a subset of $\{B_0Q\}$. The two
schemes below differ in how much they select and in what kind of economics they use.
Recursive identification picks out exactly one point, using a claim about the timing of
decisions within the period. Sign restrictions pick out a region, using a claim about the
direction of responses.

### Result R-7.2: recursive identification and the role of the ordering

Let $\Sigma$ be symmetric positive definite. There is exactly one lower triangular matrix
$P$ with strictly positive diagonal such that $\Sigma = PP^\top$, the Cholesky factor, and
setting $B_0 = P$ leaves no rotational freedom. Reading $u_t = P\varepsilon_t$ row by row,

$$
u_{1t} = P_{11}\varepsilon_{1t},\qquad
u_{2t} = P_{21}\varepsilon_{1t} + P_{22}\varepsilon_{2t},\qquad
u_{3t} = P_{31}\varepsilon_{1t} + P_{32}\varepsilon_{2t} + P_{33}\varepsilon_{3t},
$$

so the first variable responds within the period to its own shock alone and the last
responds to everything. Let $\Pi$ be a permutation matrix reordering the variables and
$\tilde P$ the Cholesky factor of $\Pi\Sigma\Pi^\top$. The impact matrix implied by the
reordering, expressed in the original variable order, is $B_0^{(\Pi)} =
\Pi^\top\tilde P\,\Pi$, which satisfies $B_0^{(\Pi)}B_0^{(\Pi)\top} = \Sigma$ and equals
$P$ only when $\Sigma$ is diagonal. The two are linked by the rotation $Q =
P^{-1}\Pi^\top\tilde P\Pi$, so the ordering is not a labelling convention but a selection
of a different point on the orbit of R-7.1.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Existence and uniqueness. Write the $(i,j)$ entry of $PP^\top$ for $j \leq i$,
remembering that $P_{ab} = 0$ whenever $b > a$, so the sum truncates at $\min(i,j) = j$:

$$
\Sigma_{ij} = \sum_{s=1}^{m} P_{is}P_{js} = P_{ij}P_{jj} + \sum_{s=1}^{j-1}P_{is}P_{js}.
$$

Solve for the unknowns in the order $(1,1), (2,1), (2,2), (3,1), \dots$, column by column
within each row. For $i = j$,

$$
P_{jj} = \sqrt{\Sigma_{jj} - \sum_{s=1}^{j-1}P_{js}^2},
$$

and for $i > j$,

$$
P_{ij} = \frac{1}{P_{jj}}\left(\Sigma_{ij} - \sum_{s=1}^{j-1}P_{is}P_{js}\right).
$$

Every quantity on the right has already been determined when it is needed, so the
recursion determines $P$ completely. The square root is the only place a choice appears
and the positive diagonal requirement removes it; the quantity under the root is positive
precisely because $\Sigma$ is positive definite, being the conditional variance of the
$j$-th variable given the first $j-1$, that is the Schur complement of the leading
$(j-1)\times(j-1)$ block. No rotational freedom survives: if $PQ$ is lower triangular then
$Q = P^{-1}(PQ)$ is a product of lower triangular matrices and so lower triangular, and a
lower triangular orthogonal matrix is diagonal with entries $\pm 1$, which the positive
diagonal requirement fixes at $+1$. So $Q = I_m$.

What the triangularity assumes. The recursion says the first variable's innovation is
driven by the first structural shock alone, so that variable does not react within the
period to anything else, while the last variable loads on every shock and so is assumed to
see everything and respond immediately. This is a claim about which decisions are made
before which others inside one observation period. Putting a policy rate last says the
central bank observes this month's output and prices before setting the rate, and that
output and prices cannot respond to the rate until next month. Putting it first says the
opposite on both counts.

Why the ordering changes the answer. With $\Pi$ the permutation and $\tilde P$ the
Cholesky factor of $\Pi\Sigma\Pi^\top$,

$$
B_0^{(\Pi)}B_0^{(\Pi)\top} = \Pi^\top\tilde P\Pi\Pi^\top\tilde P^\top\Pi
= \Pi^\top\tilde P\tilde P^\top\Pi = \Pi^\top\Pi\Sigma\Pi^\top\Pi = \Sigma,
$$

using $\Pi^\top\Pi = I_m$, so the reordered scheme fits exactly as well. But
$\Pi^\top\tilde P\Pi$ is not lower triangular in the original order, so by the uniqueness
just proved it cannot equal $P$ unless it happens to be triangular, which for a
permutation that actually moves something requires $\Sigma$ diagonal. The linking matrix
$Q = P^{-1}\Pi^\top\tilde P\Pi$ is orthogonal because $QQ^\top = P^{-1}\Sigma P^{-\top} =
I_m$.

How large the disagreement is. The two-variable case is explicit. For

$$
\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_1^2 & \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2\\
\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 & \sigma_2^2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
P = \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_1 & 0\\ \rho\sigma_2 & \sigma_2\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\end{pmatrix},
$$

the impact effect of the second shock on the first variable is zero by construction.
Reversing the order makes that same impact effect $\rho\sigma_1$. Nothing in the
likelihood distinguishes $0$ from $\rho\sigma_1$: both reproduce $\Sigma$ to the last
digit. The disagreement is therefore governed by how far $\Sigma$ is from diagonal. With
uncorrelated innovations every ordering gives the same diagonal $P$ and the question
evaporates; with strongly correlated innovations the orderings can imply opposite signs on
impact.
:::

Recursive identification buys a point estimate at the price of a timing assumption that
is often hard to defend and always consequential. The alternative weakens the assumption
and accepts a weaker conclusion.

### Result R-7.3: sign restrictions and the accepted set

Fix a reduced-form draw $(B,\Sigma)$, let $P$ be any matrix with $PP^\top = \Sigma$, and
let $\mathcal{S}$ be a finite list of inequality restrictions on the responses
$\Psi_hPq$ of the system to a candidate impact vector $q$, imposed over a finite set of
horizons. Define

$$
\mathcal{Q}(B,\Sigma) = \left\{q : \|q\| = 1,\; \Psi_hPq \text{ satisfies } \mathcal{S}
\text{ at every restricted } h\right\}.
$$

Draw $q$ as the first column of a rotation $Q$ that is uniform on the orthogonal group,
keep the draw when $q \in \mathcal{Q}(B,\Sigma)$ and discard it otherwise. The retained
draws are a sample from

$$
p(B,\Sigma,q \mid Y, \mathcal{S}) \;\propto\;
p(B,\Sigma \mid Y)\,\mu(q)\,\mathbb{1}\{q \in \mathcal{Q}(B,\Sigma)\},
$$

with $\mu$ the Haar measure, and the acceptance rate estimates
$\Pr(\mathcal{S}\mid Y) = \mathbb{E}_{B,\Sigma}[\mu(\mathcal{Q}(B,\Sigma))]$, the
posterior probability that a structural explanation drawn at random satisfies the imposed
economics. Generically $\mathcal{Q}$ has positive measure rather than being a single
point, so the restrictions deliver set identification: the spread of the accepted
responses does not vanish as $T \to \infty$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

The rotation must be uniform, and a QR decomposition delivers that. Let $Z$ be $m \times
m$ with independent standard Normal entries and $Z = QR$ its QR decomposition with $R$
upper triangular. The density of $Z$ is $p(Z) \propto \exp(-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}
Z^\top Z)$, which depends on $Z$ only through $Z^\top Z$. Replacing $Z$ by $ZO$ for a
fixed orthogonal $O$ gives $(ZO)^\top(ZO) = O^\top Z^\top ZO$, whose trace is unchanged,
so $p(ZO) = p(Z)$; and $Z \mapsto ZO$ has Jacobian determinant $|\det O|^m = 1$ and so
preserves Lebesgue measure. Hence $Z$ and $ZO$ have the same distribution for every
orthogonal $O$. That right-invariance transfers to the factor $Q$, and the only
probability measure on the orthogonal group invariant under right multiplication is the
Haar measure, which is what uniform means here.

One detail spoils this if ignored. The QR decomposition is not unique: for any diagonal
$D$ with entries $\pm 1$, $(QD)(DR)$ is another valid factorisation with $DR$ still upper
triangular. Numerical routines return whichever sign convention the underlying Householder
algorithm produces, which is not the uniform one. The fix is to impose the convention
explicitly by forcing the diagonal of $R$ to be positive,

$$
D = \operatorname{diag}\!\left(\operatorname{sign}(R_{11}),\dots,\operatorname{sign}(R_{mm})\right),
\qquad Q \leftarrow QD,
$$

which is the single line `Qm = Qm * np.sign(np.diag(Rm))` in the code below. Without it
the draws are still orthogonal and still reproduce $\Sigma$, but they are not uniform, so
the accepted set would be weighted in a way nobody intended.

Why any $q$ is admissible before the restriction. By R-7.1, $Pq$ for a unit vector $q$ is
the first column of some $PQ$ with $PQ(PQ)^\top = \Sigma$, so every unit $q$ gives an
impact vector consistent with the reduced form. The likelihood is constant over the
sphere, which is the identification problem stated as a group action, and the restriction
cuts the sphere down.

What the accepted sample is. Three cases can occur for a given draw. If $\mathcal{Q}$ is
empty the reduced-form draw is incompatible with the restrictions and contributes nothing.
If $\mathcal{Q}$ is a single point the shock is point identified for that draw, which
essentially never happens with inequality restrictions. Generically $\mathcal{Q}$ has
positive Haar measure. Proposing one $q$ per reduced-form draw and discarding failures is
accept-reject sampling from the displayed joint distribution, exactly as in Lecture 3 with
an indicator playing the role of the envelope, and the acceptance probability conditional
on $(B,\Sigma)$ is $\mu(\mathcal{Q}(B,\Sigma))$. Averaging over the posterior gives the
unconditional acceptance rate, which is therefore an estimate of $\Pr(\mathcal{S}\mid Y)$
and a number worth reporting rather than a diagnostic: an acceptance rate of one fifth says
four fifths of the structural explanations the data cannot rule out were ruled out by the
economics.

Two consequences deserve emphasis. First, the quantiles of the accepted responses mix two
kinds of uncertainty. Even if $(B,\Sigma)$ were known exactly the spread over
$\mathcal{Q}$ would remain, so the bands do not shrink to a line as $T$ grows. Reading such
a band as a credible interval about a single true response is a mistake; it is a credible
interval about a set. Second, redrawing $Q$ repeatedly until every reduced-form draw yields
an acceptance would give each $(B,\Sigma)$ equal weight regardless of how large its
admissible set is, effectively dividing by $\mu(\mathcal{Q}(B,\Sigma))$, which is a
different and generally unintended posterior. Keep one proposal per draw. Finally, the
uniform measure on rotations is itself a prior. It is conventional rather than innocuous,
and there is a literature on how much the resulting bands depend on it.
:::

The two results are not alternatives on a scale of sophistication. R-7.2 makes a strong
assumption and returns a number; R-7.3 makes a weak assumption and returns a set. Which is
preferable depends on whether the timing claim or the sign claim is easier to defend in
the application at hand, and @sec-empirical runs both so the difference can be priced.

## Data: output, prices and the policy rate, 1960 to 2019 {#sec-data}

The chapter's dataset is the monthly FRED macroeconomic snapshot,
`data/fred_macro_monthly.parquet`, the same file and the same three series used in Lecture
6: industrial production, the consumer price index and the effective federal funds rate.
The two index levels enter as one hundred times the monthly log difference, so a unit
reads as one percent per month, and the funds rate enters in percentage points. No other
series is used anywhere in this chapter.

The window is February 1960 to December 2019, $719$ months, of which $707$ are usable once
twelve lags are consumed. The sample stops before the pandemic deliberately. The April 2020
observation is a fourteen percent monthly fall in industrial production, more than fourteen
standard deviations from the mean, and a Gaussian system fitted through it would inflate
the whole residual covariance and therefore every impulse response in the chapter. That is
a modelling choice worth stating rather than hiding, and Lecture 12 supplies the
stochastic-volatility machinery that would let the sample include it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-macro-panel
#| fig-cap: "The three series of the chapter over the estimation window. Output growth and inflation are monthly log changes in percent; the funds rate is in percentage points."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(7.5, 6.2), sharex=True)
for ax, nm, lab in zip(axes, var_names,
                       ["IP growth (% per month)", "CPI inflation (% per month)",
                        "federal funds rate (%)"]):
    ax.plot(mac.index, mac[nm], lw=0.7, color="steelblue")
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.6)
    ax.set_ylabel(lab, fontsize=9)
axes[0].set_title("Output, prices and the policy rate, 1960-2019")
axes[-1].set_xlabel("date")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(mac.describe().loc[["mean", "std", "min", "max"]].round(3).to_string())
print(f"first-order autocorrelations: "
      f"{np.round([mac[c].autocorr(1) for c in var_names], 3)}")
```

Industrial production grows by $0.200$ percent a month on average with a standard
deviation of $0.744$, and inflation averages $0.303$ percent a month, about $3.6$ percent
a year, with a standard deviation of $0.312$. The funds rate averages $4.996$ percent and
ranges from $0.07$ to $19.1$, the upper end being the Volcker disinflation of 1981. The
first-order autocorrelations, $0.342$, $0.627$ and $0.990$, explain why the funds rate
dominates the persistence of the system and why the impulse responses below are still some
way from their long-run values after three years.

The asymmetry in those three transformations is deliberate and has consequences later. A
monthly policy rate in levels is close to a unit root over a sixty-year sample containing
one long disinflation and two long spells at the zero lower bound, which is why the
Minnesota prior mean on its own first lag is one while the two differenced series take
zero. It is also why the impulse responses of @sec-empirical are reported as levels for
output and prices, obtained by cumulating the growth-rate responses, and in percentage
points for the rate: a cumulated fall of half a percent in the level of industrial
production is the quantity a policy discussion is about, while a response of monthly
output growth of $-0.05$ at horizon six is not.

## Empirical analysis: what does a rate surprise do? {#sec-empirical}

### The reduced-form posterior

The reduced-form model is the Minnesota-shrunk system of Lecture 6, estimated here by
simulation rather than at its posterior mean, because the identification exercises need
draws of $\Sigma$ as well as of $B$. The prior is the Normal-diffuse pair: the Minnesota
Normal prior of Result R-6.3 on $\operatorname{vec}B$, and an independent inverse-Wishart
$\Sigma \sim \mathcal{IW}(I_m, m+2)$ on the covariance. The two full conditionals are

$$
\operatorname{vec}B \mid \Sigma, Y \sim \mathcal{N}(b_n, P_n^{-1}),
\qquad
P_n = V_0^{-1} + \Sigma^{-1}\otimes X^\top X,
\qquad
b_n = P_n^{-1}\!\left[V_0^{-1}b_0 + (\Sigma^{-1}\otimes X^\top)\operatorname{vec}Y\right],
$$

$$
\Sigma \mid B, Y \sim \mathcal{IW}\!\left(S_0 + (Y-XB)^\top(Y-XB),\; \nu_0 + T_{\text{eff}}\right),
$$

the first by completing the square in $\operatorname{vec}B$ against the generalised
least-squares quadratic, the second by adding the residual cross-product to the prior
scale and the sample size to the prior degrees of freedom. Cycling between them is the
two-block Gibbs sampler of Lecture 4 applied to a system, and it is needed rather than a
closed form because the Minnesota prior variance does not factor as a Kronecker product
with $\Sigma$, as the end of the R-6.3 derivation explained. The prior mean on own first
lags is $(0,0,1)$, zero for the two differenced series and one for the funds rate.

```{python}
def minn_prior_pieces(m, p, sig, lam1, lam2, lam_c, rw_mean):
    k = 1 + m * p
    B0, V = np.zeros((k, m)), np.zeros((k, m))
    V[0, :] = lam_c
    for ell in range(1, p + 1):
        for j in range(m):
            row = 1 + (ell - 1) * m + j
            for i in range(m):
                V[row, i] = (lam1 / ell**2 if i == j else
                             lam1 * lam2 / ell**2 * sig[i]**2 / sig[j]**2)
            if ell == 1:
                B0[row, j] = rw_mean[j]
    return B0, V

sig_var = D_var.std(axis=0, ddof=1)
B0_p, V0_p = minn_prior_pieces(m_var, p_var, sig_var, 0.05, 0.5, 100.0,
                               np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]))
prec0 = np.diag(1.0 / V0_p.ravel(order="F"))
b0 = B0_p.ravel(order="F")
XtX, XtY = X_var.T @ X_var, X_var.T @ Y_var
nu0, S0 = m_var + 2, np.eye(m_var)

n_sweep, burn = 3000, 500
Sigma_state = Sigma_ols.copy()
B_draws = np.empty((n_sweep - burn, k_var, m_var))
S_draws = np.empty((n_sweep - burn, m_var, m_var))
for r in range(n_sweep):
    inv_sigma = np.linalg.inv(Sigma_state)
    Vpost = np.linalg.inv(prec0 + np.kron(inv_sigma, XtX))
    bpost = Vpost @ (prec0 @ b0 + (XtY @ inv_sigma).ravel(order="F"))
    Lp = np.linalg.cholesky((Vpost + Vpost.T) / 2)
    Bd = (bpost + Lp @ rng.standard_normal(k_var * m_var)).reshape(k_var, m_var, order="F")
    res_d = Y_var - X_var @ Bd
    Sigma_state = stats.invwishart.rvs(df=nu0 + T_eff, scale=S0 + res_d.T @ res_d,
                                       random_state=rng)
    if r >= burn:
        B_draws[r - burn], S_draws[r - burn] = Bd, Sigma_state

B_mean = B_draws.mean(axis=0)
eig_post = np.abs(np.linalg.eigvals(companion(B_mean, m_var, p_var))).max()
print(f"{len(B_draws)} retained sweeps")
print(f"sum of |lag coefficients|: OLS {np.abs(B_ols[1:]).sum():.3f}, "
      f"posterior mean {np.abs(B_mean[1:]).sum():.3f}")
print(f"largest |posterior mean - OLS|: {np.abs(B_mean - B_ols).max():.4f}")
print(f"largest companion eigenvalue at the posterior mean: {eig_post:.4f}, "
      f"half-life {np.log(0.5) / np.log(eig_post):.1f} months")
print("posterior mean of Sigma:")
print(pd.DataFrame(S_draws.mean(axis=0), index=var_names, columns=var_names).round(4))
```

With $707$ usable observations for $37$ coefficients per equation the prior is present but
no longer decisive, which is the honest situation for a sixty-year sample: the total
absolute lag-coefficient mass falls from $8.352$ under least squares to $5.168$ under the
posterior mean, a real compression but nothing like the fourfold reduction the ten-year
window of Lecture 6 produced. The posterior mean of $\Sigma$ is close to the least-squares
residual covariance, as it must be with a prior contributing five degrees of freedom
against a sample of seven hundred. The largest companion eigenvalue is $0.9821$, a
half-life of $38.3$ months, so the three-year horizon used below is the medium run rather
than the end of the story.

The sampler is doing more here than producing a point estimate. Every identification
exercise below needs a draw of $\Sigma$, because the impact matrix is a function of
$\Sigma$ and nothing else, so the posterior uncertainty in the responses comes from the
coefficient draws and the covariance draws jointly. Reporting a Cholesky factor of the
posterior mean covariance and a response computed at the posterior mean coefficient would
give a line with no band and would understate the uncertainty twice over, once by
discarding the spread of $(B,\Sigma)$ and once, as R-7.3 makes precise, by ignoring the
spread across rotations that no amount of sampling removes.

### Recursive identification, with the rate last and then first

The two orderings compared are the two standard ones. Ordering the funds rate last says
the Federal Reserve sets this month's rate having seen this month's output and inflation,
while output and prices cannot respond until next month. This is what most of the recursive
monetary literature assumes and it is defensible at monthly frequency, since production and
price-setting decisions are largely made before the month's policy meeting. Ordering it
first says the reverse. By R-7.2 both reproduce $\Sigma$ exactly, and the data are silent
between them. Responses of the two differenced variables are cumulated into responses of
their levels, because a response of output growth of $-0.05$ at horizon six is hard to
read while a cumulated fall of half a percent in the level of industrial production is
exactly what a policy discussion is about.

```{python}
def chol_impact(Sigma, order, m):
    P = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma[np.ix_(order, order)])
    B = np.zeros((m, m))
    B[np.ix_(order, order)] = P                     # undo the permutation
    return B

def to_level(ir):
    out = ir.copy()
    out[:, 0, :] = np.cumsum(ir[:, 0, :], axis=0)   # level of industrial production
    out[:, 1, :] = np.cumsum(ir[:, 1, :], axis=0)   # price level
    return out

H_r = 36
order_last, order_first = np.array([0, 1, 2]), np.array([2, 0, 1])
lvl_last = np.zeros((len(B_draws), H_r + 1, m_var))
lvl_first = np.zeros_like(lvl_last)
for i in range(len(B_draws)):
    lvl_last[i] = to_level(irf(B_draws[i], chol_impact(S_draws[i], order_last, m_var),
                               H_r, m_var, p_var))[:, :, 2]
    lvl_first[i] = to_level(irf(B_draws[i], chol_impact(S_draws[i], order_first, m_var),
                                H_r, m_var, p_var))[:, :, 2]

q_last = np.quantile(lvl_last, [0.16, 0.5, 0.84], axis=0)
q_first = np.quantile(lvl_first, [0.16, 0.5, 0.84], axis=0)
row_lab = ["IP level (%)", "price level (%)", "funds rate (pp)"]
print("posterior median response to the recursively identified policy shock")
for tag, qq in [("rate ordered last", q_last), ("rate ordered first", q_first)]:
    print(f"  {tag}:")
    print(pd.DataFrame(qq[1, [0, 6, 12, 24, 36]].T, index=row_lab,
                       columns=[f"h={h}" for h in (0, 6, 12, 24, 36)]).round(3))
print(f"impact response of the IP level, 68% band, ordered last: "
      f"[{q_last[0, 0, 0]:.3f}, {q_last[2, 0, 0]:.3f}]")
print(f"impact response of the IP level, 68% band, ordered first: "
      f"[{q_first[0, 0, 0]:.3f}, {q_first[2, 0, 0]:.3f}]")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-orderings
#| fig-cap: "Responses to a recursively identified policy shock, with the funds rate ordered last (left) and first (right). Shaded areas are 68% posterior bands. The first two rows cumulate the growth-rate responses into level responses."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(10, 7.2), sharex=True)
for col, (qq, ttl) in enumerate([(q_last, "funds rate ordered last"),
                                 (q_first, "funds rate ordered first")]):
    for row in range(3):
        ax = axes[row, col]
        hor = np.arange(H_r + 1)
        ax.fill_between(hor, qq[0, :, row], qq[2, :, row], color="steelblue", alpha=0.25)
        ax.plot(hor, qq[1, :, row], color="steelblue", lw=1.6)
        ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
        if col == 0:
            ax.set_ylabel(row_lab[row], fontsize=9)
        if row == 0:
            ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=10)
        if row == 2:
            ax.set_xlabel("horizon (months)")
fig.suptitle("The same policy shock under two timing assumptions")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The two columns are R-7.2 made visible on real data. With the rate ordered last the
response of the industrial production level is zero on impact by construction, turns
negative and drifts down to $-0.346$ percent after three years. With the rate ordered
first output rises by $0.117$ percent on impact, keeps rising to $0.166$ percent at six
months, and crosses zero only in the third year, ending at $-0.168$ percent. One ordering
says a surprise tightening cuts output; the other says it raises output for a year and a
half. The 68 percent bands do not overlap on impact, $[0.000, 0.000]$ against $[0.092,
0.143]$, so this is not a difference the sample size could resolve. It is the identifying
assumption talking, exactly as R-7.2 predicts from a residual correlation of $0.180$.

The middle row is worse, and instructively so. Under both orderings the price level rises
after a contractionary shock, by $0.422$ percent at three years ordered last and $0.547$
percent ordered first. This is the price puzzle of Sims (1992), one of the best-known
failures of the recursive monetary VAR: a shock identified as a tightening is followed by
higher inflation. The standard explanation is that the funds-rate innovation in a
three-variable system is not a clean policy surprise but is contaminated by the central
bank's reaction to information about future inflation that the three variables do not
contain, so the shock is partly an inflation forecast. The bottom row shows the shock
itself: the rate jumps $0.442$ percentage points on impact ordered last and decays to
$0.218$ by three years, a persistent but not permanent tightening under either ordering.

The honest summary of this subsection is that recursive identification on this panel
produces one response that depends entirely on the ordering and one that is puzzling under
every ordering. Neither is a failure of estimation. Both schemes reproduced $\Sigma$
exactly, both used the same posterior draws, and the bands around each are perfectly
ordinary posterior bands. What differs is a claim about what the Federal Reserve saw
before it acted, and R-7.2 says that claim selects a point on the orbit rather than
estimating one. An economist who prefers the rate-last ordering is entitled to the
left-hand column, but must say out loud that the number came from the assumption and not
from the sixty years of data.

### Sign restrictions on the impact month

The alternative replaces the timing assumption with a statement about direction. A
contractionary monetary policy shock is one that, on impact, raises the federal funds rate
and does not raise either output or the price level. We impose exactly that, no more, and
in particular nothing at all about any later horizon, so whatever the responses do after
the first month is an implication of the estimated dynamics rather than of the
restriction. The algorithm is the accept-reject rotation sampler of R-7.3.

```{python}
def sign_accepted(B_draws, S_draws, n_horizon, H, m, p, rng):
    kept, n_try = [], 0
    for i in range(len(B_draws)):
        P = np.linalg.cholesky(S_draws[i])
        cand = irf(B_draws[i], P @ haar_rotation(m, rng), H, m, p)
        n_try += 1
        for s in (1.0, -1.0):
            probe = s * cand[:n_horizon, :, 0]      # first column = candidate policy shock
            if (probe[:, 2] > 0).all() and (probe[:, 1] <= 0).all() and (probe[:, 0] <= 0).all():
                kept.append(to_level(s * cand)[:, :, 0])
                break
    return np.array(kept), n_try

acc_impact, n_try_impact = sign_accepted(B_draws, S_draws, 1, H_r, m_var, p_var, rng)
acc_three, n_try_three = sign_accepted(B_draws, S_draws, 3, H_r, m_var, p_var, rng)
fan_q = np.quantile(acc_impact, [0.05, 0.16, 0.5, 0.84, 0.95], axis=0)

print(f"restrictions on impact only:     accepted {len(acc_impact)}/{n_try_impact} "
      f"= {len(acc_impact)/n_try_impact:.3f}")
print(f"restrictions over three months:  accepted {len(acc_three)}/{n_try_three} "
      f"= {len(acc_three)/n_try_three:.3f}")
print("\nposterior median of the accepted set, impact restrictions only")
print(pd.DataFrame(fan_q[2, [0, 6, 12, 24, 36]].T, index=row_lab,
                   columns=[f"h={h}" for h in (0, 6, 12, 24, 36)]).round(3))
print(f"IP level trough: {fan_q[2, :, 0].min():.3f} percent at horizon "
      f"{int(fan_q[2, :, 0].argmin())}")
print(f"price level at h=36: {fan_q[2, 36, 1]:.3f} percent, "
      f"90% band [{fan_q[0, 36, 1]:.3f}, {fan_q[4, 36, 1]:.3f}]")
print(f"IP level at h=12: 68% band [{fan_q[1, 12, 0]:.3f}, {fan_q[3, 12, 0]:.3f}], "
      f"90% band [{fan_q[0, 12, 0]:.3f}, {fan_q[4, 12, 0]:.3f}]")
print(f"share of accepted draws with a negative IP level at h=12: "
      f"{(acc_impact[:, 12, 0] < 0).mean():.3f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-sign-fan
#| fig-cap: "Fan chart of the accepted set of responses to a contractionary monetary policy shock identified by sign restrictions on the impact month only. Dark band 68%, light band 90%, line the median of the accepted draws."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.9))
hor = np.arange(H_r + 1)
for row, (ax, lab) in enumerate(zip(axes, row_lab)):
    ax.fill_between(hor, fan_q[0, :, row], fan_q[4, :, row], color="firebrick", alpha=0.15)
    ax.fill_between(hor, fan_q[1, :, row], fan_q[3, :, row], color="firebrick", alpha=0.32)
    ax.plot(hor, fan_q[2, :, row], color="firebrick", lw=1.8)
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel("horizon (months)"); ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=10)
fig.suptitle("Sign-restricted responses to a contractionary policy shock")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The restrictions bite hard. Only about one rotation in five satisfies three inequalities
on the impact month, and extending the same restrictions over the first three months
roughly halves the acceptance rate again. By R-7.3 that acceptance rate is itself an
estimate: it is the posterior probability, under a uniform prior over rotations, that a
structural explanation of these data drawn at random is a contractionary policy shock of
this kind. Reporting it is part of reporting the result: a scheme that accepts nine
rotations in ten has barely restricted anything, and a scheme that accepts one in a
thousand is either imposing a great deal or is in conflict with the reduced form, and the
difference between those two cases is not visible in the bands alone.

What comes out is the textbook monetary transmission that the recursive schemes failed to
deliver. The industrial production level falls, reaching a trough of $-0.680$ percent at
eleven months, and recovers only partially, to $-0.577$ percent, by three years. The
median price level falls steadily to $-0.459$ percent at three years, so the price puzzle
is gone from the median: it was an artefact of forcing the
policy shock to be the funds-rate innovation, and once we ask only for a shock that raises
the rate and does not raise prices in the impact month, the admissible rotations imply a
disinflation. Honesty requires adding that the 90 percent band on the price level at three
years runs from $-1.004$ to $+0.135$ percent, so a rising long-run price level has been
made unlikely rather than excluded. Over the same accepted set $97.1$ percent of draws
have a negative output level at one year, with a 68 percent band from $-1.095$ to
$-0.238$ percent, so the direction survives even though nothing was imposed past the
impact month.

The bands are the point of the exercise. They are wider than the recursive ones and should
be, because they carry two kinds of uncertainty at once. Part is posterior uncertainty
about $B$ and $\Sigma$, which shrinks with the sample. The rest is the spread across
admissible rotations, which does not: with an infinite sample, three sign restrictions on
impact would still leave a set of observationally equivalent structural models, and the
fan would settle at the width of that set rather than collapsing to a line.

```{python}
#| label: fig-three-schemes
#| fig-cap: "The response of the industrial production level to a contractionary policy shock under three identification schemes on identical reduced-form draws. Only the identifying assumption differs."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(hor, q_last[1, :, 0], "-", color="steelblue", lw=1.8,
        label="recursive, rate ordered last")
ax.plot(hor, q_first[1, :, 0], "--", color="seagreen", lw=1.8,
        label="recursive, rate ordered first")
ax.plot(hor, fan_q[2, :, 0], "-", color="firebrick", lw=1.8,
        label="sign restrictions on impact")
ax.fill_between(hor, fan_q[1, :, 0], fan_q[3, :, 0], color="firebrick", alpha=0.18)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("horizon (months)"); ax.set_ylabel("response of the IP level (%)")
ax.set_title("One reduced form, three identifying assumptions, three answers")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"IP level at h=12: ordered last {q_last[1, 12, 0]:.3f}, "
      f"ordered first {q_first[1, 12, 0]:.3f}, sign-restricted {fan_q[2, 12, 0]:.3f}")
print(f"IP level at h=36: ordered last {q_last[1, 36, 0]:.3f}, "
      f"ordered first {q_first[1, 36, 0]:.3f}, sign-restricted {fan_q[2, 36, 0]:.3f}")
```

Three lines, one data set, one posterior for $(B,\Sigma)$. At twelve months the recursive
scheme with the rate last says output is $0.122$ percent below trend, the same scheme with
the rate first says it is $0.107$ percent above, and the sign-restricted median says
$0.670$ percent below. The spread across the three lines is not sampling error and would
not shrink with more data. It is the price of the identifying assumption, and the only way
to argue about it is in economic terms.

## Discussion: the fit is the same, the shocks are not {#sec-discussion}

The central bank asked what an unexpected tightening does, and the chapter's answer is
that the data narrow the question without answering it. Three schemes applied to one
posterior gave a twelve-month output response of $-0.122$, $+0.107$ and $-0.670$ percent.
Only the third is the textbook answer, and the third is the one whose assumption is
weakest, which is the reverse of the usual relationship between assumption and conclusion
and worth sitting with.

The check that the machinery is doing what R-7.1 says, rather than quietly fitting the
data differently under each scheme, is direct. Every scheme must reproduce the same
$\Sigma$ and therefore the same reduced-form residuals, which means the same likelihood
and the same forecasts; what must differ is the structural shock series
$\varepsilon_t = B_0^{-1}u_t$ recovered from them.

```{python}
#| label: fig-shock-series
#| fig-cap: "The monetary policy shock series implied by three identification schemes, recovered from identical reduced-form residuals. Twelve-month moving averages for legibility."
schemes = {"ordered last": chol_impact(S_draws.mean(axis=0), order_last, m_var),
           "ordered first": chol_impact(S_draws.mean(axis=0), order_first, m_var)}
P_mean = np.linalg.cholesky(S_draws.mean(axis=0))
for _ in range(2000):                               # one admissible rotation, impact signs
    Qc = haar_rotation(m_var, rng)
    cand = irf(B_mean, P_mean @ Qc, 1, m_var, p_var)
    hit = [s for s in (1.0, -1.0)
           if s * cand[0, 2, 0] > 0 and s * cand[0, 1, 0] <= 0 and s * cand[0, 0, 0] <= 0]
    if hit:
        schemes["sign restricted"] = hit[0] * (P_mean @ Qc)
        break

U_post = Y_var - X_var @ B_mean
dates = mac.index[p_var:]
eps = {}
for lab, B0 in schemes.items():
    col = 2 if lab.startswith("ordered") else 0     # policy shock column
    eps[lab] = (U_post @ np.linalg.inv(B0).T)[:, col]
    print(f"{lab:>16}: max |B0 B0' - Sigma| = "
          f"{np.abs(B0 @ B0.T - S_draws.mean(axis=0)).max():.3e}, "
          f"shock sd {eps[lab].std():.4f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for lab, e in eps.items():
    ax.plot(dates, pd.Series(e, index=dates).rolling(12).mean(), lw=1.1, label=lab)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
ax.set_ylabel("identified policy shock, 12-month mean"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Identical residuals, three different histories")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

labs = list(eps)
print("correlations between the implied shock series:")
print(pd.DataFrame(np.corrcoef(np.array([eps[l] for l in labs])),
                   index=labs, columns=labs).round(3))
```

All three impact matrices reproduce the posterior mean covariance to machine precision, so
the reduced-form residuals, the likelihood and every forecast are identical under the
three schemes. The recovered shock histories are not. The two recursive series correlate
at $0.983$, so with residual correlations as mild as these the ordering moves the shock
history only a little; the sign-restricted series correlates with them at $0.335$ and
$0.250$, sharing about a tenth of its variance with the first and less with the second.
It is a substantially
different linear combination of the same residuals, and it attributes the tightening
episodes of the sample to different months. The identification problem is not an
abstraction about matrices. It decides which month in 1981 counts as a policy surprise.

What should a practitioner report? Not a single impulse response function. The minimum
honest output of a structural vector autoregression is the reduced-form posterior, the
identifying restrictions stated before the responses were looked at, the acceptance rate
when the scheme is an inequality one, and a band that is labelled as set identification
where it is set identification. The three figures of @sec-empirical are all computed from
one posterior sample, and the difference between them is a fact about assumptions that a
reader cannot recover from any one of them alone.

Two limitations follow, and the second is the binding one. The first is that sign
restrictions on three variables are weak, and the honest report is the acceptance rate
together with the band: about one rotation in five survived, so four fifths of the
observationally equivalent explanations were excluded by three inequalities, and the rest
remain. Adding variables, a commodity price index in particular, or restrictions at more
horizons, narrows the set at the cost of stronger assumptions, and Lecture 10 asks the
prior question of what the restrictions have to say in order to license a causal claim at
all.

The second limitation is that every result above assumed one set of coefficients for sixty
years. The window contains the Volcker disinflation, the Great Moderation and two spells at
the zero lower bound, and the estimated system averages a monetary policy rule across all
of them. A coefficient is not a constant of nature: the responsiveness of the policy rate to
inflation in 1980 is not its responsiveness in 2015, just as a bank's market beta in 2008 is
not its beta in 2000. A structural response computed from an average rule describes no
period in the sample. Lecture 8 drops the assumption, writing the coefficients themselves as
a latent state that evolves over time, and estimating them with the Kalman filter and
forward filtering backward sampling.

## Exercises

These are the chapter's practice questions; the [Week 7 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/07-bvar-identification.qmd) works through them and adds the
lab.

1. By hand. For $m = 2$ write the general orthogonal matrix as a rotation by angle
   $\theta$ possibly composed with a reflection, and show directly that the one-dimensional
   family $P(\theta)$ traces every solution of $\Sigma = B_0B_0^\top$. Then impose one sign
   restriction on the impact response of the first variable and describe the admissible set
   of $\theta$ as an arc, giving its length as a function of the correlation $\rho$. State
   what happens to that length as $\rho \to \pm 1$.

2. Computational. Take the Gibbs draws of @sec-empirical and compute the forecast error
   variance decomposition under the recursive scheme with the rate ordered last, using
   $\text{FEVD}_{ij}(h)$ equal to the cumulated squared responses of variable $i$ to shock
   $j$ divided by the same sum over all shocks. Report the policy shock's share of the
   funds rate, output and inflation variance at horizons $0$, $12$ and $36$ with 68 percent
   bands, then repeat under the reverse ordering and say which cells change and why.

3. On real data. Add the ten-year Treasury yield from the same file as a fourth variable and
   rerun the sign-restricted exercise, requiring in addition that the long yield does not
   fall on impact. Report the new acceptance rate, compare it with the three-variable one
   using the interpretation of R-7.3, and say in one paragraph whether the extra restriction
   or the extra variable did more to narrow the identified set.

Exercise 1 is the one to attempt before the session, since it makes the orbit of R-7.1
concrete in the only case where it can be drawn. Exercises 2 and 3 are written for the
session itself and reuse the code of @sec-empirical.

## Reading and references

The reduced-form system posterior, the matricvariate Normal likelihood and the
Normal-diffuse prior behind the two full conditionals of @sec-empirical follow Bauwens
(2013), Chapter 4, and SGPE Lecture 4, pages 3 to 23; the derivations of the
inverse-Wishart posterior and of the conjugate alternative are worked in the Week 7
exercise session. The Cholesky argument of R-7.2 and the ordering dependence are standard;
Koop, Chapter 6, states them in the notation used here. R-7.3 follows Rubio-Ramírez,
Waggoner and Zha (2010), which supplies the Haar-uniform rotation argument and the
algorithm, and the set-identification reading of the accepted band follows the same paper's
discussion. The price puzzle is Sims (1992). The data are the monthly FRED series
distributed with this course as a repository snapshot.

The explanations and exercises are adapted to this course's notation and weekly structure;
consult the cited originals for the full treatments.

Bańbura, Giannone and Reichlin (2010), "Large Bayesian Vector Auto Regressions," *Journal
of Applied Econometrics*. Rubio-Ramírez, Waggoner and Zha (2010), "Structural Vector
Autoregressions: Theory of Identification and Algorithms for Inference," *Review of
Economic Studies*. Sims (1992), "Interpreting the Macroeconomic Time Series Facts,"
*European Economic Review*. Koop, *Bayesian Econometrics*, ch. 6. Chan, Koop, Poirier and
Tobias, *Bayesian Econometric Methods* (2nd ed.), ch. 18.
